questions.stem: Which sequence shows the stimulus-response model in the correct order?
options: Receptor, stimulus, effector, control centre, response
Stimulus, control centre, receptor, effector, response
Stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector, response
Stimulus, effector, control centre, receptor, response
questions.explanation: A change (stimulus) is detected by a receptor, which sends a message to the control centre. The control centre signals an effector, which produces the response. The effector acts after the control centre, not before it.

questions.stem: What is meant by negative feedback in homeostasis?
options: A response that holds a variable at exactly one value so that it never fluctuates
A response that reverses the change that triggered it, moving a variable back towards its set point
A response that amplifies the change that triggered it, moving a variable further from its set point
A response that stops the receptor from detecting any further change in the variable
questions.explanation: In negative feedback the response counteracts the stimulus, so the variable returns towards its set point. Variables still fluctuate within a narrow range around the set point; they are not held perfectly constant. Amplifying a change describes positive feedback.

questions.stem: How do the nervous and endocrine systems compare in the way they coordinate responses?
options: Nervous responses are fast and brief; endocrine responses are slower and usually last longer
Nervous responses are slow and long-lasting; endocrine responses are fast and short-lived
Nervous responses reach every cell; endocrine responses reach only nearby cells
Nervous responses use chemicals only; endocrine responses use electrical impulses only
questions.explanation: Nerve impulses travel quickly along neurons to specific effectors, so responses are rapid and short-lived. Hormones travel in the blood or lymph to target cells, so their effects are slower to start but last longer. Nerves do use chemical neurotransmitters at synapses, so neither system is purely electrical.

questions.stem: Why must the human body keep factors such as temperature and pH within narrow limits?
options: Nerve impulses can travel only when the blood pH is exactly at its set point
Enzymes that control metabolism work only within a narrow tolerance range
Red blood cells carry oxygen only when the blood is at its exact set point
Cells can divide only when temperature and pH are exactly at their set points
questions.explanation: Metabolic reactions are catalysed by enzymes, and each enzyme works well only within a tolerance range of temperature and pH. Outside this range enzyme activity falls and enzymes may denature. The other processes do not require one exact value.

questions.stem: Receptors in the aorta and carotid arteries detect changes in the concentration of carbon dioxide in the blood. What type of receptor are they?
options: Thermoreceptors
Nociceptors
Chemoreceptors
Mechanoreceptors
questions.explanation: Chemoreceptors respond to chemical stimuli such as the concentration of carbon dioxide, oxygen or hydrogen ions. Mechanoreceptors respond to pressure, touch or stretch, not chemical concentration.

questions.stem: A person touches a very hot pan and immediately feels pain. Which receptors produce the sensation of pain?
options: Mechanoreceptors
Nociceptors
Photoreceptors
Chemoreceptors
questions.explanation: Nociceptors respond to stimuli intense enough to damage tissue, such as extreme heat, and their signals are perceived as pain. Thermoreceptors detect ordinary temperature changes, but the pain itself comes from nociceptors.

questions.stem: What is the function of the dendrites of a neuron?
options: To receive signals from receptors or other neurons and carry them towards the cell body
To carry impulses away from the cell body towards the axon terminals
To release neurotransmitter from vesicles into the synaptic cleft by exocytosis
To insulate the axon so that the impulse can jump between the gaps in it
questions.explanation: Dendrites are branched extensions that receive incoming signals and conduct them towards the soma. The axon carries impulses away from the cell body, and the myelin sheath provides insulation.

questions.stem: Why does a nerve impulse travel faster along a myelinated axon than along an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter?
options: Myelin contains extra sodium channels, so each section of axon depolarises more quickly
Myelin conducts the electrical current itself, like a copper wire wrapped around the axon
Neurotransmitter is released at every node, relaying the impulse further along the axon
Action potentials occur only at the nodes of Ranvier, so the impulse jumps from node to node
questions.explanation: Myelin insulates the axon, so ion movement and depolarisation can happen only at the nodes of Ranvier. The impulse jumps between nodes (saltatory conduction), which is much faster. Myelin is an insulator, not a conductor, and neurotransmitter is released only at axon terminals.

questions.stem: A neuron has its cell body in the spinal cord and an axon that runs to a muscle in the leg. Which type of neuron is it?
options: Interneuron
Afferent neuron
Motor neuron
Sensory neuron
questions.explanation: Motor neurons carry impulses from the central nervous system to effectors such as muscles. Sensory (afferent) neurons carry impulses from receptors towards the central nervous system.

questions.stem: What happens at the axon membrane during the depolarisation phase of an action potential?
options: Voltage-gated sodium channels open and Na⁺ ions diffuse out of the axon
Voltage-gated sodium channels open and Na⁺ ions diffuse into the axon
Voltage-gated potassium channels open and K⁺ ions diffuse into the axon
The sodium-potassium pump moves Na⁺ ions rapidly into the axon
questions.explanation: When the membrane reaches threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open and Na⁺ diffuses in down its concentration gradient, making the inside positive. The sodium-potassium pump moves Na⁺ out of the cell, not in.

questions.stem: After the peak of an action potential, what returns the inside of the axon to a negative potential?
options: K⁺ ions diffusing out of the axon through voltage-gated channels
Na⁺ ions diffusing out of the axon through voltage-gated channels
K⁺ ions pumped into the axon by the sodium-potassium pump
Na⁺ ions pumped into the axon by the sodium-potassium pump
questions.explanation: During repolarisation, voltage-gated potassium channels open and K⁺ diffuses out, removing positive charge from inside the axon. The sodium-potassium pump restores the ion distribution afterwards, but it is too slow to cause repolarisation.

questions.stem: A weak stimulus just above threshold and a much stronger stimulus are applied to the same sensory neuron. How does the nervous system detect the difference?
options: The stronger stimulus produces one longer-lasting action potential in the neuron
The weaker stimulus produces action potentials that travel more slowly along the axon
The stronger stimulus produces a higher frequency of action potentials of the same size
The stronger stimulus produces action potentials of a larger size in the same neuron
questions.explanation: Action potentials are all-or-none: once threshold is reached, every action potential in a neuron has the same size. Stimulus strength is coded by how often action potentials are fired, and by how many neurons are stimulated, not by their size.

questions.stem: When an action potential reaches an axon terminal, how is neurotransmitter released into the synaptic cleft?
options: Sodium ions carry it across the cleft from the presynaptic membrane
Vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release it by exocytosis
It diffuses out through protein channels in the presynaptic membrane
Receptors on the postsynaptic membrane pull it across the synaptic cleft
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitter is stored in vesicles in the axon terminal. The arriving action potential causes the vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their contents by exocytosis, after which the neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft.

questions.stem: Why can a nerve impulse cross a synapse in one direction only?
options: The synaptic cleft is too narrow for neurotransmitter to diffuse back towards the presynaptic cell
Myelin around the postsynaptic cell blocks impulses from travelling back to the presynaptic cell
The postsynaptic cell breaks down all neurotransmitter before it can bind to any receptor there
Only presynaptic terminals release neurotransmitter, and only postsynaptic cells have its receptors
questions.explanation: Vesicles of neurotransmitter are found only in the presynaptic axon terminal, and the receptors that bind it are on the postsynaptic membrane, so the signal can pass only one way. Diffusion can occur in any direction, so the width of the cleft is not the reason.

questions.stem: Neurotransmitter binds to receptors that are ligand-gated ion channels on the postsynaptic membrane. What is the immediate effect?
options: The channels open, changing the membrane potential of the postsynaptic cell
The neurotransmitter enters the postsynaptic cell and travels along its axon
Vesicles in the postsynaptic cell release more neurotransmitter into the cleft
The myelin sheath of the postsynaptic cell depolarises along its whole length
questions.explanation: Binding of the neurotransmitter opens the ion channels, so ions flow across the postsynaptic membrane and change its potential. This conversion of a chemical signal into an electrical one is a form of signal transduction. The neurotransmitter itself does not travel along the postsynaptic neuron.

questions.stem: How do hormones travel from endocrine glands to their target cells?
options: Through ducts that open onto target cells
By diffusion across the synaptic cleft
In the circulatory or lymphatic system
Along the axons of motor neurons
questions.explanation: Endocrine glands are ductless and secrete hormones into body fluids, which carry them in the circulatory or lymphatic system to target cells throughout the body. Delivery along axons to a synapse is how the nervous system signals.

questions.stem: Adrenaline reaches almost every cell in the body, yet only some cells respond to it. Why?
options: Only target cells have the genes needed to absorb adrenaline into the nucleus
Only target cells display receptors that are specific to adrenaline
Only cells near the adrenal glands receive enough adrenaline to respond
All other cells break adrenaline down as soon as it reaches them
questions.explanation: A hormone affects only cells that display receptors specific to it, because binding to the receptor is what triggers a change in cell activity. Hormones circulate throughout the body in the blood, so distance from the gland does not decide which cells respond.

questions.stem: Cell X displays 20 000 receptors for a hormone and cell Y displays 5000. Both are exposed to the same concentration of the hormone. What would be expected?
options: Cell Y responds more strongly, because each of its receptors binds more of the hormone
Both respond equally, because the response depends only on hormone concentration
Cell X responds more weakly, because its many receptors compete for the hormone
Cell X responds more strongly, because sensitivity increases with the number of receptors
questions.explanation: A cell's sensitivity to a hormone is directly related to the number of receptors it displays: more receptors means more hormone binding and a greater response. Each receptor binds a hormone molecule in the same way, so cell Y's receptors do not compensate.

questions.stem: After a meal, beta cells in the pancreas detect a rise in blood glucose and release insulin, which travels in the blood and causes liver and muscle cells to take up glucose. In a feedback-control diagram, what is the effector?
options: Beta cells of the pancreas
Insulin carried in the blood
The rise in blood glucose
Liver and muscle cells
questions.explanation: The effectors are the cells that carry out the response, here liver and muscle cells taking up glucose. The beta cells act as both receptor and control centre, insulin is the communication pathway, and the rise in glucose is the stimulus.

questions.stem: When body temperature falls, the hypothalamus sends impulses along motor neurons to skeletal muscles, which begin to shiver. In a feedback-control diagram, what role do the motor neurons play?
options: The receptors that detect the fall in body temperature
The control centre that compares temperature with the set point
The effectors that generate heat by contracting rapidly
The communication pathway from the control centre to the effector
questions.explanation: Motor neurons carry the message from the control centre (the hypothalamus) to the effectors (skeletal muscles), so they are a communication pathway. The muscles are the effectors, and thermoreceptors are the receptors.

questions.stem: Brown adipose tissue helps endotherms produce heat because its cells contain:
options: many chloroplasts that capture radiant energy and convert it into body heat
many ribosomes that make proteins which store heat for release in cold weather
many mitochondria that release much of their energy as heat rather than as ATP
large stores of fat that insulate the body without using any metabolic energy
questions.explanation: Brown fat cells are packed with mitochondria, and in these mitochondria much of the energy from respiration is released as heat instead of being used to make ATP. This is non-shivering thermogenesis. Insulation is mainly the role of white fat, fur and feathers.

questions.stem: Which is a structural thermoregulatory feature, rather than a behavioural or physiological response?
options: A koala pressing its body against a cool tree trunk
A dog panting rapidly on a hot afternoon
A possum shivering on a frosty night
A thick layer of blubber beneath a seal's skin
questions.explanation: Blubber is a permanent body structure that provides insulation. Pressing against a cool surface is behavioural, while panting (evaporative heat loss) and shivering (thermogenesis) are physiological mechanisms.

questions.stem: Emperor penguins huddle tightly through the Antarctic winter, each bird gaining heat produced by its neighbours. Which thermoregulatory behaviour is this?
options: Kleptothermy
Aestivation
Torpor
Vasoconstriction
questions.explanation: Kleptothermy means gaining heat from the body of another animal, as huddling birds do from each other. Torpor is a temporary drop in metabolic rate and body temperature, and vasoconstriction is a physiological response, not a behaviour.

questions.stem: Which statement describes aestivation?
options: A drop in body temperature and metabolic rate lasting only a few hours on a cold night
Gaining heat from the body of another animal by close physical contact
A period of dormancy with a lowered metabolic rate during hot, dry conditions
A period of dormancy with a lowered metabolic rate during a cold winter
questions.explanation: Aestivation is dormancy that helps an animal survive heat and drought by reducing metabolic rate and water loss. Dormancy through a cold winter is hibernation, and a short overnight drop in body temperature is daily torpor.

questions.stem: Some small marsupials, such as dunnarts, lower their body temperature and metabolic rate for several hours on cold nights, then rewarm by morning. What is this response called?
options: Daily torpor
Hibernation
Aestivation
Kleptothermy
questions.explanation: A short-term, controlled drop in metabolic rate and body temperature lasting hours is daily torpor, which saves energy when food is scarce or nights are cold. Hibernation is a much longer period of torpor through a season.

questions.stem: Why is torpor especially common in small endotherms such as hummingbirds and small marsupials?
options: Their low SA:V ratio means they cannot lose heat, so they must reduce heat production
Their small brains cannot keep controlling body temperature for a full 24 hours
Their fur or feathers trap so much heat that they must cool down every night
Their high SA:V ratio means they lose heat quickly, so staying warm uses a lot of energy
questions.explanation: Small animals have a large surface area relative to their volume, so they lose heat rapidly and need a high metabolic rate to stay warm. Torpor lowers their body temperature and saves energy when food is scarce. Small animals have a high, not low, SA:V ratio.

questions.stem: Red kangaroos lick their forearms on hot days. How does this help them lose heat?
options: Saliva evaporating from the skin removes heat from blood flowing in the forearms
Saliva forms an insulating layer that slows heat gain from the hot surroundings
Licking causes vasoconstriction, which keeps warm blood away from the skin
Saliva reflects sunlight, so less heat is gained by radiation through the skin
questions.explanation: Evaporation of water requires energy, which it takes as heat from the skin and the blood vessels beneath it. This is evaporative heat loss, the same principle as sweating and panting. Vasoconstriction would reduce heat loss, not increase it.

questions.stem: On a hot day, the arterioles that supply the skin capillaries dilate. How does this lower body temperature?
options: The capillaries move closer to the skin surface so that they can release heat
The dilated vessels release sweat, which evaporates and carries heat away
More blood flows close to the skin surface, so more heat is lost to the surroundings
Less blood reaches the skin surface, so less heat is carried away from the core
questions.explanation: Vasodilation of arterioles increases blood flow through the skin capillaries, so more heat is transferred to the surroundings by radiation, conduction and convection. The capillaries do not move; more blood simply flows through them. Sweat comes from sweat glands, not blood vessels.

questions.stem: Which part of the brain is the control centre for thermoregulation in humans?
options: Medulla oblongata
Cerebellum
Hypothalamus
Posterior pituitary
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus receives information from thermoreceptors in the skin and in the hypothalamus itself, compares body temperature with the set point and coordinates the response. The posterior pituitary releases hormones such as ADH but does not control temperature.

questions.stem: Which pair of responses occurs when a person's core body temperature falls below the set point?
options: Sweating and vasodilation in the skin
Shivering and vasoconstriction in the skin
Sweating and vasoconstriction of the skin arterioles
Shivering and vasodilation in the skin
questions.explanation: Shivering generates heat by rapid muscle contraction, and vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to the skin, reducing heat loss. Sweating and vasodilation are responses to a rise in body temperature.

questions.stem: Why does a person overheat more easily when exercising on a hot, humid day than on a hot, dry day?
options: Humid air conducts heat into the body through the layer of sweat on the skin
Sweat evaporates more slowly in humid air, so less heat is removed from the skin
Humid air causes the skin's arterioles to constrict, so less heat reaches the skin
Sweat glands stop producing sweat when the humidity of the air is high
questions.explanation: Sweating cools the body only when the sweat evaporates. In humid air the rate of evaporation is lower, so sweat drips off instead of removing heat. Sweat glands keep producing sweat, which is why people become drenched in humid conditions.

questions.stem: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is released from the posterior pituitary. Which parts of the nephron does it act on?
options: The loop of Henle and the glomerulus
The distal tubule and collecting duct
The glomerulus and Bowman's capsule
The proximal tubule and loop of Henle
questions.explanation: ADH targets cells of the distal tubule and collecting duct, making them more permeable to water. Filtration occurs at the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule, and is not controlled by ADH.

questions.stem: How does ADH increase the reabsorption of water in the kidney?
options: It increases the rate at which blood is filtered through the glomerulus
It increases the number of sodium pumps in the walls of the glomerulus
It increases the number of aquaporins in the membranes of collecting duct cells
It causes the collecting duct cells to actively pump water molecules into the blood
questions.explanation: ADH causes more aquaporins (water channel proteins) to be inserted into the membranes of distal tubule and collecting duct cells, so more water moves by osmosis back into the blood. Water is never actively pumped; it moves by osmosis.

questions.stem: After a long run without drinking, a person's blood becomes more concentrated. Which sequence describes the feedback response?
options: Osmoreceptors in the kidney detect it, less ADH is released, and a large volume of dilute urine forms
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect it, less ADH is released, and a small volume of concentrated urine forms
Thermoreceptors in the skin detect it, more ADH is released, and a large volume of dilute urine forms
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect it, more ADH is released, and a small volume of concentrated urine forms
questions.explanation: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the increased solute concentration, and more ADH is released from the posterior pituitary. More water is reabsorbed, so less, more concentrated urine is produced. Less ADH would have the opposite effect on urine.

questions.stem: Which plant hormone triggers the closing of stomata when a plant is short of water?
options: Gibberellic acid
Ethylene
Abscisic acid
Indoleacetic acid
questions.explanation: Abscisic acid is produced when a plant is under water stress and causes the guard cells to close the stomata, reducing water loss. Auxin mainly controls cell elongation and tropisms.

questions.stem: Why do stomata close when abscisic acid acts on guard cells?
options: The guard cells divide rapidly and fill the space of the stomatal pore
The guard cells lose ions and water, become flaccid and close the pore
The guard cells take in ions and water, swell and close the pore
The cuticle over the guard cells thickens and seals the stomatal pore
questions.explanation: Abscisic acid causes ions to leave the guard cells, so water follows by osmosis. The guard cells lose turgor and become flaccid, closing the pore. Guard cells that take up water become turgid and open the stoma.

questions.stem: Why do many plants in hot, dry habitats have a thick, waxy cuticle?
options: It reduces the loss of water by evaporation from the leaf surface
It increases the rate of gas exchange through the epidermal cells
It stores water that the plant can use during long dry periods
It absorbs extra light so photosynthesis can continue in drought
questions.explanation: The waxy cuticle is waterproof, so it reduces evaporation from the epidermis and helps the plant keep its water balance. Water is stored in vacuoles and other tissues, not in the cuticle.

questions.stem: A pot plant left in the sun on a hot day wilts. What has happened in its cells?
options: Their cuticles have dissolved, so the cells have lost their shape
Their chloroplasts have stopped, so the cells have used up glucose
Their vacuoles have lost water, so the cells have lost turgor
Their vacuoles have taken in water, so the cell walls have burst
questions.explanation: The large central vacuole holds water that keeps the cell turgid and pressing against its wall, which supports soft tissues. When water loss exceeds uptake, vacuoles shrink, turgor falls and the plant wilts. Plant cell walls stop cells bursting when they take in water.

questions.stem: Using area of a circle = πr², what is the stomatal density of a leaf peel with a mean of 25 stomata per field of view, if the field of view is 0.40 mm in diameter?
options: About 156 per mm²
About 200 per mm²
About 50 per mm²
About 63 per mm²
questions.explanation: The radius is 0.20 mm, so the area is π × 0.20² ≈ 0.126 mm², and the density is 25 ÷ 0.126 ≈ 200 per mm². Using the diameter as the radius gives about 50 per mm², and dividing by the diameter gives about 63.

questions.stem: Stomatal densities (per mm²) were measured on three species. P: upper surface 0, lower surface 210. Q: upper 360, lower 0. R: upper 5, lower 40, with stomata in sunken pits. Which matches each species to its likely habitat?
options: P: moist woodland shrub; Q: arid shrubland; R: floating water plant
P: moist woodland shrub; Q: floating water plant; R: arid shrubland
P: floating water plant; Q: arid shrubland; R: moist woodland shrub
P: arid shrubland; Q: moist woodland shrub; R: floating water plant
questions.explanation: Floating leaves can exchange gases only through the upper surface, which is in contact with the air. Few, sunken stomata reduce water loss in dry habitats. Many plants of moist habitats have stomata mainly on the shaded lower surface, which loses less water.
